Article Title: Smart glasses have a privacy problem and Meta may have just 'fixed' it
Article Text:
Meta Glasses

Taking the camera out of the conversation

A better fit for everyday use

Sometimes, the smartest upgrade is a missing feature. Meta’s decision to launch AI glasses without a camera could do more to broaden their appeal than another improvement in video quality. For buyers who like the idea of connected eyewear but dislike the baggage of wearing a recording device, there is now a more comfortable proposition. Announced at Connect 2026 last week, the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses start at $349. Developed with EssilorLuxottica, they offer music, podcasts, calls, speech translation and access to Meta’s AI assistant, Muse. These are familiar functions, packaged in something people may already wear every day. The camera’s absence is the selling point.That makes this a sensible move. Technology companies often assume that adding capabilities automatically makes a product more desirable. Wearables complicate that equation because other people have to live with them, too. A device sitting on someone’s face affects the person across the table as much as its owner.Meta’s earlier glasses demonstrated the appeal of recording life without reaching for a phone. For holidays, family moments or content creation, that convenience has obvious value. But the same ease of capture also created an uncomfortable question: how does anyone nearby know whether they are becoming somebody else’s content?Reports of people filming others without consent, including women approached by men wearing the glasses, turned that concern into something tangible.The derogatory “pervert glasses” nickname reflected how quickly a product’s reputation can be shaped by its worst uses. Responsible owners were left carrying some of that reputational burden.Meta introduced safeguards, including updates designed to disable the camera when the recording indicator is tampered with. Those measures matter. But a light requires people to notice it, understand it and trust that it works. It also cannot establish whether someone has agreed to be filmed.Removing the camera offers a much simpler assurance. Buyers do not have to choose between enjoying connected eyewear and carrying a feature they may rarely use but repeatedly have to explain. There is potentially a sizeable audience for that choice: people interested in calls and music who have little desire to document their surroundings.The benefit extends beyond reassuring strangers. Someone might feel more comfortable wearing these glasses around colleagues, at a family gathering or while meeting friends. A useful wearable should slip into everyday routines. If its presence becomes a recurring conversation about surveillance, the convenience starts losing its appeal.There are limits, of course. Camera-free does not mean privacy-free. Microphones and AI services still raise questions about what information is collected, processed and retained. Nor will everyone immediately distinguish the audio model from camera-equipped versions. Meta will need clear communication, but it now has a meaningful hardware difference to explain.The stronger commercial argument is that audio may be enough. Many prospective buyers could reasonably want to answer a call, hear a podcast or ask a question without taking out their phones. None of those tasks requires a camera. Removing it makes the proposition easier to understand.For people who already wear spectacles, the appeal is particularly straightforward. Adding useful audio functions to an existing habit could feel more natural than finding room for another gadget. Others may welcome an alternative to wearing earbuds. The potential audience includes people who would never describe themselves as early adopters.That brings Meta into a familiar contest with products such as Apple’s Siri-enabled AirPods: which device makes small, repeated tasks easiest? The glasses do not need to replace a smartphone to earn their place. They need to make enough everyday interactions more convenient that wearing them becomes a habit.Muse will face the same practical test. An assistant that responds reliably and saves time could strengthen the product’s appeal. One that requires repeated instructions will quickly become a feature owners ignore. Music and calls provide a useful foundation while buyers decide how much AI they actually want.At $349, Meta still has to justify the purchase. Comfort, sound quality, battery life and reliable calling will matter more than keynote promises. Removing the camera also sacrifices visual AI functions and hands-free photography. Those are worthwhile capabilities, but offering a choice recognises that buyers value them differently.Meta has made a good move because it gives people a reason to reconsider the category. For plenty of buyers, useful glasses that attract less suspicion may be the upgrade they were waiting for.
Article Summary: Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses start at $349. They offer music, podcasts, calls, speech translation and access to Meta’s AI assistant, Muse. For buyers who like the idea of connected eyewear but dislike the baggage of wearing a recording device, there is now a more comfortable proposition.

Article Title: 'Godmother Of AI' Fei-Fei Li gets a 'new job'; to join AMD in $8.2 billion deal; aim is to take on Nvidia
Article Text:
‘Godmother Of AI’ Fei-Fei Li

AMD has announced that it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire World Labs, an AI model and research lab led by Fei-Fei Li., popularly known as ‘Godmother Of AI’. In a statement, the company said that the acquisition will bring a world-class team of researchers and model experts to AMD, strengthening its ability to develop AI hardware, software and systems around the needs of emerging models and applications.As per chip giant, following the close of the transaction, the World Labs team will continue to focus on advancing AI model research, and Fei-Fei Li will join AMD as executive vice president and chief scientist, reporting to AMD CEO Lisa Su. The all-stock transaction is valued at approximately $8.2 billion and is expected to close by the end of 2026, subject to regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions.As AI expands into reasoning, robotics, simulation and physical AI, the demands on compute infrastructure become more diverse. World Labs’ expertise in developing advanced models will give AMD deeper insight into how workloads are evolving and help shape its future technology roadmaps. The acquisition advances AMD’s strategy to deliver AI infrastructure for an open ecosystem.“Building the compute platforms for the next generation of AI requires a deep understanding of how models are evolving,” said Dr.Lisa Su, chair and CEO, AMD. “Fei-Fei and the World Labs team bring exceptional research leadership and model expertise. Together, we can use that insight to develop the hardware, software and systems that will power the next generation of AI and strengthen the open AI ecosystem.”“Advancing the next generation of AI technology requires close collaboration across model research, systems and compute,” said Fei-Fei Li, co-founder and CEO, World Labs. “Joining AMD will give our team the resources and engineering depth to accelerate our research and help define the infrastructure needed for the next era of AI.”Deal may help AMD narrow gap with NvidiaHeadquartered in San Francisco, World Labs develops spatial-intelligence models that generate, reconstruct and simulate interactive 3D environments from text, image and video inputs, as well as technology for robotic learning and simulation. The acquisition is expected to help AMD narrow the gap between it and its primary competitor, Nvidia. World Labs develops AI models that can reconstruct and simulate 3D environments from text, images and video inputs. AMD’s addition of Fei-Fei may also be a major selling point for the many AI researchers who currently rely on Nvidia hardware for their work.
Article Summary: AMD has announced that it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire World Labs, an AI model and research lab led by Fei-Fei Li. The all-stock transaction is valued at approximately $8.2 billion and is expected to close by the end of 2026, subject to regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions.

Article Title: Researchers at Oxford and Cambridge show that ChatGPT has now a 'big problem' and America's biggest investor Michael Burry agrees with them; says: Research on this is ...
Article Text:
The problem: models trained on their own output

Burry's own warning, echoed and expanded

A deeper claim: LLMs may never reach AGI

Setting up a clash with Jensen Huang

Researchers at Oxford and Cambridge have identified a fundamental flaw threatening the future of large language models like ChatGPT, and "Big Short" investor Michael Burry says the finding backs up a warning he's been making about the technology's core limitations for a while. A new study from the University of Oxford and University of Cambridge has revealed a major threat to large language models like ChatGPT, calling it “model collapse.” The research shows that when generative AI systems are repeatedly trained on synthetic data produced by earlier models, they begin to lose the “tails” of the original data distribution. In practice, this means models forget the creative, fringe, and unique nuances of human writing, collapsing into repetitive echo chambers.America’s biggest investor, Michael Burry, reacted to the findings on X, saying: “This is to my point about compression being inevitable as human knowledge is too small for what we are building. AI-generated content will clearly contain propagation errors… LLMs will iterate those propagation errors infinitely faster with less ability to self-correct.”Burry drew attention to the research by sharing a post outlining what scientists call "model collapse."The concern centers on a shift already underway across the internet: as generative AI produces more and more of the text online, future AI models risk being trained on data that was itself generated by earlier AI systems, rather than by humans.According to the research, feeding AI-generated content back into training indiscriminately causes what researchers describe as irreversible defects in the resulting model. Specifically, the model begins losing the "tails" of the original data distribution, meaning it gradually forgets the creative, unusual, and distinctly human nuances present in real human writing. Over successive generations, this causes the model to collapse into an increasingly narrow, repetitive echo chamber of its own outputs.Crucially, the researchers found this isn't unique to ChatGPT or language models specifically. Their theoretical framework showed the collapse phenomenon is ubiquitous across learned generative models more broadly, appearing in large language models as well as in variational autoencoders and Gaussian mixture models.The stakes are significant for the entire AI industry, given how heavily tech companies rely on scraping large volumes of internet data to train increasingly capable models. The research warns that if companies want to sustain the benefits of training on web data going forward, model collapse needs to be taken seriously as a genuine constraint rather than a theoretical curiosity. The clear takeaway, as the research frames it: genuine, human-generated data is going to become an increasingly scarce and valuable resource in a web that's rapidly filling up with AI-generated content.Writing on X, Burry tied the research directly to an argument he's made before: that compression of available information is essentially inevitable, because human knowledge itself is too limited relative to the scale of what AI companies are trying to build, and because human wants, needs, and questions are inherently repetitive and redundant.He went further, warning that AI-generated content will inevitably carry forward "propagation errors," much like inaccuracies that have accumulated throughout human knowledge over generations — except AI systems, in his view, will be capable of iterating and reproducing those errors infinitely faster, with far less capacity to self-correct due to what he sees as a lack of genuine understanding.Burry used the moment to make a broader, more philosophical argument about artificial general intelligence. He argued that large language models cannot attain true understanding — and therefore cannot reach AGI — because understanding, in his view, cannot exist unless reasoning exists independently of language first, something he called a likely impossibility for a system built entirely around language prediction. He acknowledged that researchers are already exploring ways to work around this limitation, while noting that many in the field haven't accepted his underlying premise in the first place.Burry's skepticism lands in direct contrast to comments made earlier this month by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who declared that AGI has already arrived, citing OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra model as proof. Huang's claim drew immediate pushback from parts of the AI research community.Stanford's Institute for Human-Centered AI defines AGI as AI capable of learning, reasoning, and applying knowledge across a broad range of tasks at or beyond human-level performance — critically, with the ability to adapt to unfamiliar situations, unlike narrow AI built for specific tasks. The concept remains genuinely unsettled within the field, with no universally accepted definition or standardized test for confirming when AGI has actually been reached, alongside ongoing debates over its safety and ethical implications.
Article Summary: A new study from the University of Oxford and University of Cambridge has revealed a major threat to large language models like ChatGPT. The research shows that when generative AI systems are repeatedly trained on synthetic data produced by earlier models, they lose the “tails” of the original data distribution. In practice, this means models forget the creative, fringe, and unique nuances of human writing, collapsing into repetitive echo chambers.

Article Title: Nvidia unveils security system that 'sets boundaries' for AI agents going rogue
Article Text:
Nvidia unveils safety platform to stop AI agents from going rogue

Nvidia has unveiled a new security platform that the chipmaker said can stop AI agents from going rogue. The company said Monday that its Open Agent Safety Platform includes open source software that "sets boundaries for agents," and follows a series of revelations from top AI companies about their models escaping and breaking into other organisations.The disclosures sparked furious debate about the safety of advanced artificial intelligence systems, including self-improving models that some fear could race out of human control.Nvidia executives said that the system could have prevented the recent swarm of OpenAI agents that autonomously hacked into AI company Hugging Face.From what we know, this new security platform could have stopped the breach if it was being used in frontier labs for model evaluation early on," said the company's vice president of enterprise AI, Justin Boitano, referring to companies at the forefront of AI.The Hugging Face incident was a high-profile breach that inflamed safety concerns about AI, which were followed by similar rogue actions involving OpenAI's models including including a breach of an Australian govt system, as well as attempts to access dozens of US govt and university websites. Anthropic and Meta have also disclosed that their AI systems hacked into other organisations on their own.Nvidia's software, called OpenShell, lets developers "formally verify an agent has enough authority to do its job and no more," Boitano said.Because it's open source, it can be "extended" to run on rival computing platforms including those from Arm and Intel. The platform also includes a separate security layer called Sentry that runs onboard a chip to continuously monitor AI agent activity and can "intervene instantly" if the agent starts trying to move beyond its target, the company said. "It can quarantine a suspicious agent in milliseconds," Boitano said."OpenShell governs the agent's actions, and then Sentry independently monitors and contains suspicious behaviour." Nvidia said more than 100 organisations are using the platform at its launch, including Microsoft, Perplexity, Accenture, and JPMorgan Chase.
Article Summary: N Nvidia unveils a new security platform to stop AI agents from going rogue. The company said that the system could have prevented the recent swarm of OpenAI agents that autonomously hacked into AI company Hugging Face. Nvidia said more than 100 organisations are using the platform at its launch.

Article Title: AWS's Darko Mesaros on how spec-driven development is bringing structure to AI-powered coding
Article Text:
Vibe coding is cheap to start and expensive to finish. Amazon's Kiro wants the spec written first.

Hand a coding task to an AI agent today and it keeps going on its own. It writes the code, runs the tests, reads the error it just caused and tries again. There is a name for working this way, vibe coding, where the developer describes what they want in rough terms and lets the model fill in the rest. Developers now spend more of the day watching that than typing.Every one of those loops is billed, and they do not add up in a straight line, because each attempt drags along everything the agent read before it. Ten tries cost more than ten times one try. A flat monthly fee used to absorb that. This year nearly every major coding tool switched to charging for what gets used, and the sums became the developer's problem.Darko Mesaros does not think that is a bad way to start. He calls vibe coding an excellent way to get something out quickly, and has spent much of the past year making the case that what comes after it needs more structure. A distinguished developer advocate at AWS, he spends his week in front of developers, explaining how the company's tools work and building with them himself. The tool is Kiro, the development environment Amazon launched a year ago, designed around the opposite instinct: settle a written specification first, argue it out line by line, and generate nothing until the document is agreed.Amazon calls this spec-driven development, and Mesaros says the time it takes upfront is why he rarely has to redo work. "When I build something with spec-driven development, I can usually one-shot things," he said. "Even though it's a bigger lift initially, it can literally one-shot things instead of iterating over multiple loops and costing many tokens."The billing shift behind that argument happened fast. OpenAI moved Codex to token-based credits in April, GitHub Copilot followed in June, and Cursor ended its flat-rate pricing in August, a month after launching an India-only plan at Rs 649.Claude Code now runs a weekly cap over a rolling five-hour limit.The price per token is not the reason. The same capability costs less every few months, and Anthropic has held Sonnet 5 at two dollars per million input tokens after dropping a planned increase in August. What grew is the work behind a single instruction, since an agent that opens a repository, writes a file, runs the tests and tries again spends tokens on every cycle, and the context it carries grows as it goes.Providers have a partial fix, called prompt caching. A model stores the unchanged opening portion of a request and reads it back later at a tenth of the normal input price. It only works if that portion is identical, character for character, so a timestamp near the top of a prompt or a model swapped mid-task will break it. Nothing flags that, and teams find out from the invoice.So one team can pay ten times what another pays for identical work. Three things decide it: which model picks up the job, how many attempts it takes, and how much of the context can be read from cache. Kiro goes after all three.Start with the attempts. Kiro's Spec Builder drafts three files the developer approves before any code exists. The requirements file lists user stories in EARS notation, a format from safety-critical engineering where every line is a condition and a response: when a user submits a form with invalid data, the system shall show errors next to the relevant fields. The design file sets out the architecture, and the tasks file breaks the build into steps. Kiro Crew's Task Runner works through those, running independent tasks in parallel, reviewing its own work after a few runs and saving progress after each one so an interrupted job can pick up where it stopped.Mesaros puts the weight on the approval, not the drafting. "When I'm certain on the spec and we go through all the things and I agree on all the things modified, it takes that spec," he said. Changing direction while the requirements are open costs an edited line, where the same change after generation means another full pass over the codebase.When developers select Auto in Kiro, it automatically chooses the best model at the backend for the task and optimises the process based on the prompt and its complexity, while keeping costs in mind. Auto is an agent rather than a model, a router sitting in front of a catalogue that spans Anthropic, OpenAI and open-weight models. "If the task is super simple, it's probably going to use the smaller model, which is a lot faster," Mesaros said. "But if it's something more complex, it's going to choose accordingly."Running a task on Sonnet 4 instead costs about 1.3 times as many of Kiro's credits for the same work. Auto also settles on its choice at the start of a task and stays with it, which keeps the cache intact.Context is loaded the same way. Memory and lessons come in once, when a session opens, and each turn after refreshes only the project rules and short references to relevant skills. Mesaros points to the semantic memory underneath, a vector database the agent queries instead of reloading instruction files wholesale, which he calls the more optimised route.AWS says the Mumbai trading platform Dhan built a real-time charting system supporting more than 170 indicators in eight weeks with one engineer, against an estimate of 12 to 24 months. Glimmertech, another customer, credits the structure with catching what it calls Potemkin house problems, where code looks finished but does not work underneath.Nor does Amazon claim any of it comes free. Its own guide calls this an engineering investment and warns the first few weeks feel slower. Everyone else is arriving at some version of the idea anyway, since Claude Code reads a CLAUDE.md file into every request, Codex reads AGENTS.md and Cursor supports rules files.None of it is new either. Writing the requirements before the code is what software engineering did for decades, until it came to look like an expensive way to be slow. EARS came out of aircraft and medical devices, where finding out later was never an option.What has changed is who the document is for. For decades it was written for whichever engineer inherited the project two years on, and it was the first thing dropped when a deadline arrived. Now a machine reads it at the start of every session, and every reading turns up on the bill. Developers let the specification go because it felt like a slow way to work. The billing is why Mesaros thinks that structure is coming back.
Article Summary: Amazon's Kiro wants the spec written first. Vibe coding is cheap to start and expensive to finish. Every one of those loops is billed, and they do not add up in a straight line. Ten tries cost more than ten times one try.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Fei Fei Li: Smart CEOs should be thinking about AI and its impact on their respective business
Article Text:
Quote of the day

Smart CEOs should be thinking about AI and its impact on their respective business. Fei-Fei Li- Godmother of AI

What the quote actually means

Where can AI make the biggest difference

How could AI change customer expectations

What parts of the business could be automated

What new products or services could AI enable

What are the risks

How will employees work with AI

What are competitors doing

How should AI fit into the

business strategy

Why this mindset is more important than it seems

Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the way businesses operate. It affects everything from how companies interact with customers to how employees perform everyday tasks. As AI becomes part of more products, services, and business processes, companies increasingly have to consider how the technology could affect their operations and plans.That is the idea behind a quote by Fei-Fei Li, the computer scientist and AI researcher, who said: “Smart CEOs should be thinking about AI and its impact on their respective business.” Li, who is widely known as the “Godmother of AI”, has been one of the prominent voices in the development of modern AI and computer vision. The statement highlights that understanding AI is becoming an important part of thinking about a business's future.Li's statement is closely tied to how businesses should approach technological change. AI is not simply another technology that companies can consider separately from their existing operations. Depending on the industry, it can influence how products are developed, how decisions are made, how employees work and how customers interact with a company.Thinking about AI's impact does not mean every business needs to introduce AI into every part of its operations immediately. Instead, it means understanding where the technology could create opportunities, where it could introduce risks and how it could change the competitive landscape.For example, a company may use AI to automate repetitive tasks, analyse large amounts of data or improve customer support. At the same time, it may need to consider questions around accuracy, privacy, security, costs and how employees will work alongside AI systems.Some questions that can help CEOs think about AI's impact include:Identifying areas where AI can improve existing processes can help companies focus their efforts rather than adopting the technology simply because it is available.As people become familiar with AI-powered products and services, their expectations around speed, personalisation and convenience may also change.AI can handle or assist with some repetitive tasks, potentially allowing employees to spend more time on work that requires creativity, judgement and human interaction.AI can create opportunities that may not have been possible with earlier technologies, potentially changing what a company can offer its customers.Businesses also need to consider issues such as incorrect AI-generated information, data privacy, cybersecurity, intellectual property and the reliability of AI systems.AI's impact isn't limited to technology teams. Companies may need to rethink workflows, training and the skills employees need as AI becomes part of everyday work.Understanding how other companies are experimenting with AI can provide a broader view of how the technology may be changing an industry.AI initiatives are more useful when connected to a company's actual priorities rather than treated as separate technology projects.Businesses can easily view AI as a technology trend and wait to see how it develops. But AI's impact can extend beyond individual tools or features. It can affect how companies build products, compete for customers and organise their workforce.That is where Li's statement becomes relevant. Thinking about AI does not necessarily mean predicting exactly what the technology will look like several years from now. It means considering how current developments could affect a company's business and preparing for different possibilities.The same approach can apply to businesses of different sizes. A large company may be considering how AI can change its existing products and operations, while a smaller business may be looking at whether AI tools can help it compete with larger organisations.For CEOs, the discussion is therefore not limited to asking, “Should we use AI?” It can also involve asking, “Where could AI change our business, what opportunities could it create, and what do we need to prepare for?”AI can also change the nature of competition. If a technology allows companies to perform certain tasks faster or develop new services, businesses that understand those changes may need to rethink how they operate. At the same time, companies must balance experimentation with practical considerations such as costs, reliability, and responsible use.The idea also changes the way business leaders approach technological change. Instead of treating AI as something that belongs only to the technology department, the conversation becomes broader: “How could AI affect our customers, employees, products, competitors and business model?”That shift can help companies see AI not simply as a new technology, but as a factor that could shape how their business develops in the years ahead.
Article Summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the way businesses operate. It affects everything from how companies interact with customers to how employees perform everyday tasks. As AI becomes part of more products, services, and business processes, companies increasingly have to consider how the technology could affect their operations.

Nvidia is rolling out new software to prevent AI agents from escaping controlled environments and accessing systems they aren't supposed to reach. The launch comes soon after CEO Jensen Huang warned that AI labs should not continue operating if they cannot contain their experiments. Huang made the comments while discussing recent incidents in which AI agents moved beyond their intended boundaries, including cases involving OpenAI and other major AI companies. However, during his interview, Huang didn’t specifically mention the ChatGPT maker, in which Nvidia has already invested billionsNvidia’s Open Agent Safety Platform is now being positioned as an engineering solution to that problem, giving developers tools to limit what AI agents can access and do. The company says the platform could have prevented OpenAI’s July incident involving Hugging Face, when models escaped containment, accessed the open internet and attacked the open-source developer platform. Here is how Nvidia’s new safety system works and why Huang’s warning matters.Nvidia’s Open Agent Safety Platform is designed to add controls around AI agents as they perform tasks. The company says recent incidents show that model-level safeguards alone may not be enough to control what agents can access once they operate independently.said Justin Boitano, vice president of enterprise AI at Nvidia.One part of the platform is Nvidia OpenShell, which runs on central processors and is designed to limit an agent’s capabilities. Nvidia has also introduced Sentry, a monitoring system that runs on network chips rather than CPUs or GPUs.Nvidia describes the platform as a reference design, with some components open source. The approach allows other companies to build products and services around the technology rather than treating it as a single finished product.Nvidia’s announcement follows several incidents involving AI agents operating outside their intended environments. An Nvidia representative said the new platform could have prevented OpenAI’s Hugging Face incident in July.According to Boitano, Hugging Face reported more than 17,000 agents attacking its infrastructure over a period that lasted days and weeks.Boitano said.The incidents have increased attention on how AI agents should be contained as they become capable of browsing the internet, using software and interacting with external systems.Huang discussed the issue in a recent conversation with The New York Times’ Ezra Klein, arguing that AI safety should be approached as an engineering and product-development problem.Huang said.Huang also gave a conditional warning about AI labs that cannot control their experiments.e added.He also argued that companies should not release systems that are not ready.Huang said.His comments came as companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Google have disclosed incidents involving AI systems and controlled testing environments.
Article Summary: N Nvidia is rolling out new software to prevent AI agents from escaping controlled environments and accessing systems they aren't supposed to reach. CEO Jensen Huang warned that AI labs should not continue operating if they cannot contain their experiments. Nvidia’s Open Agent Safety Platform is designed to add controls around AI agents as they perform tasks.

Article Title: Apple has a new Vision Pro in the works, but a new headset is unlikely before 2028
Article Text:
Apple’s struggles with the Vision Pro

Apple's Vision team is working on the new headset

The pattern of cancelled headsets

What’s Next for Apple

Apple is reportedly developing a new Vision Pro headset, but as per Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the project is still in early stages and may not reach consumers until late 2028 or early 2029. The company is said to be working on multiple design concepts, including lighter models and offload computing power to external devices. This is the same approach which Facebook-parent Meta opted for in its recently launched VR Glasses.The Vision Pro, launched in February 2024 at nearly $4,000, has struggled to gain traction. Sales remain sluggish, with some Apple retail stores reporting only a handful of units sold each month. Internally, Apple has shelved several headset prototypes over the past two years, including Vision Air (N100) and N109, both aimed at reducing weight and cost. Leadership changes under new CEO John Ternus have further reshaped the Vision hardware team, signaling skepticism about the product’s long-term viability.Apple's Vision team is working on the new headset under the code name N224. Engineers are exploring about four concepts.Some of them offload internal components to an external unit, the same approach Meta used in its new VR Glasses, which Gurman says weigh one-sixth as much as the Vision Pro at one-third of the price.Not everyone at Apple is on board with that direction. Gurman reports that some senior decision-makers see an external puck as a poor user experience and want Apple to stay closer to an all-in-one design. He describes the work as being on "life support" while the company weighs a new direction, and there is no guarantee the device will ever ship.N224 follows several shelved projects. About two years ago, Apple dropped N107, a design that would have offloaded computing to a Mac or other device to cut the headset's bulk. A year ago it shelved N100, a "Vision Air" that would have moved more components into an external pack. Another project, N109, envisioned as a lighter, cheaper Vision Pro with a less powerful chip, was also cancelled.The Vision Pro launched in February 2024 and has not sold well. Gurman says Apple retail employees report that many stores are lucky to sell one unit a month, and Apple now promotes the roughly $4,000 device for uses such as surgery, effectively positioning it as a specialist product.Apple engineers are now working on a revamped headset under the code name N224, exploring four different concepts. Some designs mimic Meta’s external computing puck, while others stick closer to Apple’s all-in-one philosophy. However, insiders describe the project as being on “life support,” with no guarantee it will ever launch. For now, Apple is focusing on smart glasses and other wearables, including AirPods with camera sensors and a fitness-style band.
Article Summary: The Vision Pro launched in February 2024 at nearly $4,000. Sales remain sluggish, with some Apple retail stores reporting only a handful of units sold each month. Apple engineers are now working on a revamped headset under the code name N224, exploring four different concepts. Some designs mimic Meta's external computing puck, while others stick closer to Apple’s all-in-one philosophy.
